Year-round blooms, a conservatory, and a kids' splash area on 50-plus garden acres.
A 100-acre estate in Richmond, Virginia, with the reopened Gilded Age Maymont Mansion, Italian and Japanese gardens, an arboretum, a nature center, a farm, and a wildlife trail.
Hands-on science museum in the domed 1919 Broad Street Station, with a giant-screen dome theater and planetarium.
Capitol building designed by Thomas Jefferson, with free guided tours. Inside is Houdon's life-size marble statue of George Washington.
1.25-mile downtown walkway along the old Haxall and James River & Kanawha canals, with history markers. Seasonal canal boat rides run from it.
Hands-on children's museum on Broad Street with climbing, play spaces and exhibits for young kids.
Virginia's largest state park, about 7,900 acres just south of Richmond, with lakes, forest trails, biking and boat rentals.
a.l: 10301 E State Pk Rd, Chesterfield, VA 23832

a.d: Holocaust museum in a 1920s tobacco warehouse in Shockoe Bottom, founded by survivor Jay Ipson, with exhibits on Lithuanian Jewry and the camps.
Church Hill park overlooking the bend of the James River. The view, like the one from Richmond Hill in England, gave the city its name.

Three-mile, roughly 28-foot-wide concrete oceanfront boardwalk running from 2nd to 40th Streets along the Atlantic, with a separate bike path, shops, restaurants and entertainment. The original 1888 boardwalk was made of wooden planks.
A maritime discovery center in Norfolk with deck tours aboard a WWII battleship.
Sharks, sea turtles, seals, and hands-on marine exhibits, open daily 9–5.
Cypress swamps, maritime forest trails, and 1.5 miles of Chesapeake Bay beach near the 1607 landing site, with over 20 miles of hiking and biking trails.
Lighthouse from 1792, the first construction project funded by the federal government, on Fort Story at the mouth of the Chesapeake. Adults need photo ID to enter the base.
Barrier-island refuge south of the resort strip, with dune and marsh boardwalks, birding and quiet beaches.
One of the largest collections of flyable WWI and WWII aircraft in the world, in hangars on a grass airfield in rural Virginia Beach.
a.l: 1341 Princess Anne Rd, Virginia Beach, VA 23457

a.d: 175-acre garden next to Norfolk airport, with themed gardens, azalea woods and seasonal boat and tram tours.
Day trip · about 25 km from Virginia Beach. 53-acre zoo in Norfolk with giraffes, tigers, orangutans and a small train.
City park built on a former landfill: a grassy hill with city views, two lakes, a skate park and the Kids Cove playground.

Day trip · about 25 km from Virginia Beach. Remote barrier-island park between Back Bay and the ocean. It is reached only on foot, by bike, by boat or by a seasonal tram, so it has miles of empty beach.
Small museum in the 1903 life-saving station right on the boardwalk, covering shipwrecks and surf rescues.
The world's largest living-history museum, with costumed interpreters and working trades across 301 acres.
Interactive flight and space exhibits, a giant-screen IMAX theater, and hands-on aviation and space history displays.
Home of the USS Monitor Center plus a huge free lakefront park, open daily.
European-themed amusement park with rides and roller coasters, live shows, animal encounters, dining, and seasonal festivals like Howl-O-Scream and Christmas Town.
The original 1607 settlement site, with active archaeology digs and a museum of 4,000-plus recovered artifacts.
Living-history museum with full-size replicas of the three 1607 ships, a reconstructed fort and a Powhatan village.
Site of the 1781 siege where Cornwallis surrendered. Driving and walking tours cover the earthworks, cannons and Moore House.
23-mile scenic road linking Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown, running along the James and York rivers with pull-offs.
Free car-and-passenger ferry across the James River between Jamestown and Scotland, running around the clock. The crossing takes about 20 minutes.
Day trip · about 30 km from Williamsburg. Newport News museum of Virginia's native animals and plants, with indoor habitats, an outdoor boardwalk and a planetarium.
a.l: 524 J Clyde Morris Blvd, Newport News, VA 23601

a.d: Estuary park where freshwater meets the York River, with marsh and forest trails, kayaking, and fossils along the shore.
a.l: 9801 York River Park Rd, Williamsburg, VA 23188

a.d: Day trip · about 100 km from Seattle. 14,410-foot volcano with glaciers, subalpine wildflower meadows, and 260+ miles of hiking trails around Paradise and Sunrise.
Bavarian-style alpine village in the Cascades with themed shops, eateries, and year-round festivals.

Day trip · about 75 km from Seattle. Free 50-minute guided tours of the Legislative Building on Washington's Capitol Campus in Olympia, featuring Tiffany chandeliers and marble from different countries.
Day trip · about 100 km from Seattle. Diverse national park spanning alpine mountains, temperate rainforest, and 70 miles of wild Pacific coastline.
Iconic 605-foot observation tower in Seattle with panoramic views and The Loupe, a revolving glass floor about 500 feet up.
Historic public market opened in 1907, with fresh produce, local crafts, and famous fish-throwing seafood stalls.
Waterfront aquarium with marine mammals, tide-pool touch tanks, and a massive underwater dome.
One of the world's largest air and space museums, with more than 175 aircraft and spacecraft on display.
92-acre zoo in Seattle with nearly 300 animal species in award-winning naturalistic habitats.
Interactive pop-culture museum covering music, film, gaming, and sci-fi exhibits in Seattle.
Indoor-outdoor exhibit of Dale Chihuly's large-scale glass sculptures at Seattle Center.
270-foot waterfall with a public park, observation areas, trails, boardwalk, and picnic areas.
Contemporary glass art museum in Tacoma, WA, known for live glassblowing demonstrations in its Hot Shop and rotating exhibitions.
Combined zoo and aquarium with Northwest wildlife, polar bears, and sharks.
Four floors of 250+ classic and vintage cars plus interactive exhibits for all ages.
Hands-on science center under its landmark white arches at Seattle Center, with a planetarium, tropical butterfly house and dinosaur exhibits.
a.l: 200 Sue Bird Ct N, Seattle, WA 98109

a.d: Small Queen Anne hillside park with the classic postcard view of the Space Needle, downtown skyline, Elliott Bay and, on clear days, Mount Rainier.
Working locks between Puget Sound and Lake Union where visitors watch boats raised and lowered, plus a fish ladder viewing room and botanical garden.
Seattle's largest park, on Magnolia's bluffs, with forest and meadow trails, beaches and the historic West Point Lighthouse with Olympic Mountain views.
Seattle history museum in a former naval armory on Lake Union, with exhibits on the city's growth, maritime past and innovation.
Free 20-acre Japanese-style garden in south Seattle with ponds, waterfalls, stone paths and a red moon bridge.
Lake Union park built around the rusting towers of an old gasification plant, with a hill offering skyline views across the lake.
Free 230-acre University of Washington arboretum on Lake Washington with woodland trails, collections of trees and the Seattle Japanese Garden.
Giant concrete troll sculpture crushing a real Volkswagen Beetle under the Aurora Bridge in the Fremont neighborhood; kids can climb on it.
Day trip · about 75 km from Seattle. Wildlife park in the forested foothills near Eatonville where a tram tour passes bison, elk and moose roaming free, plus bear, wolf and cougar habitats.
100-acre downtown Spokane park along the Spokane River, home to Spokane Falls, a cable car ride over the falls, a historic carousel, and the Pavilion.
90-acre park with Japanese, rose, and perennial gardens plus a conservatory and duck pond.
Basalt rock formations in the Spokane River reached by a swinging suspension bridge, with riverside trails in a large state park minutes from downtown.
a.l: 9711 W Charles Rd, Nine Mile Falls, WA 99026

a.d: Day trip · about 35 km from Spokane. Washington's largest state park, with a summit road to a 1930s stone CCC lodge (Vista House) and views into three states and Canada.
a.l: 25211 N Mount Spokane Park Dr, Mead, WA 99021

a.d: Regional museum in Browne's Addition with Inland Northwest history and Plateau Native American collections, next to the historic 1898 Campbell House.
Stately gold-domed capitol building along the river.

a.n: Clay Center for the Arts & Sciences
a.d: Hands-on science exhibits, a planetarium, art galleries, and family theater shows all under one downtown roof.
A dramatic clifftop overlook 750 feet above the New River, with a nature museum, hiking trails, and jetboat rides through the gorge.
Day trip · about 75 km from Charleston WV. Ride a mine car underground with a veteran miner guide, then tour the restored coal camp village and youth museum.

Day trip · about 150 km from Charleston WV. Steam-powered trains climb switchbacks up Cheat Mountain from Cass to Bald Knob, the 4,842-foot summit of Back Allegheny Mountain. They run on the line built in 1901 to haul lumber to the mill in Cass.

a.n: New River Gorge National Park & Preserve
a.d: America's newest national park: over 70,000 acres along the New River Gorge, with scenic overlooks, waterfalls, whitewater rafting, hiking trails, and the iconic New River Gorge Bridge.

Day trip · about 110 km from Charleston WV. 4,050-acre state park on the Bluestone River Gorge with an aerial tram that descends into the gorge, plus ziplines, a splash park, horseback riding, golf and 20 hiking trails.
Day trip · about 70 km from Charleston WV. The state's largest art museum, set on over 50 acres with nature trails and a tropical plant conservatory, located in Huntington, WV.
Day trip · about 80 km from Charleston WV. West Virginia's only amusement park, a classic 1903 trolley park with the historic Big Dipper wooden coaster and a full Kiddie Land.
Day trip · about 75 km from Charleston WV. A Smithsonian-affiliated recreated Appalachian village with museums, a petting zoo, artisans, ziplines, and ropes courses.

Day trip · about 120 km from Charleston WV. Descend 120 feet below the surface on a self-guided tour of a half-mile cave loop past stalactites and stalagmites, about 45 minutes long. Discovered in 1942, the cave stays at 52 degrees year-round. A museum and gift shop are on site.
Day trip · about 130 km from Charleston WV. West Virginia's largest state park: 10,100 acres of mountains with hiking, fishing, boating, and cabins.
Day trip · about 100 km from Charleston WV. A sternwheeler ride to an Ohio River island with a reconstructed Palladian mansion, carriage rides, and a regional history museum.
Day trip · about 70 km from Charleston WV. The state's newest park, located on the shore of its largest lake: swimming, rock climbing, hiking, and biking.
Forest of about 9,300 acres a few miles from downtown, with hiking and mountain-bike trails, picnic areas and fishing ponds.
a.l: 7500 Kanawha State Forest Dr, Charleston, WV 25314

a.d: Walk-through history museum in the Culture Center at the Capitol Complex, including a re-created coal mine. Free.
a.l: Building 9, 1900 Kanawha Blvd E #435, Charleston, WV 25305

a.d: Year-round market in a 1920s railroad freight station downtown, with outdoor produce stands in season.
Large county park along Elk River with trails, a lake with pedal boats and playgrounds.
a.l: 375 Henry C Hoppy Shores Dr, Charleston, WV 25311

a.d: A walkable historic town at the meeting of two rivers, with museums, ranger programs, hiking trails, and Appalachian Trail views.
Historic Potomac river town founded in 1762, one of West Virginia's oldest, with a walkable German Street of old buildings and shops.
Stone tower on South Mountain completed in 1827, the first monument finished in honor of George Washington, reached by a short climb on the Appalachian Trail.
Day trip · about 30 km from Harpers Ferry. Site of the July 1864 battle known as 'the Battle That Saved Washington', with a visitor center, historic farms, cannons and walking trails near Frederick.
Iconic wings overlooking Lake Michigan.
190 acres home to over 2,000 animals, including gorillas, bonobos, and polar bears, plus camel rides, train rides, and a children's farm with goats.
Hands-on lakefront science and technology museum with an aquarium, touch tanks, and STEM exhibits for kids and families.

Harley-Davidson's museum in Milwaukee, the city where the brand began in 1903. It has two floors of motorcycles, rare memorabilia, and hands-on exhibits covering more than 120 years of the brand's history, plus rotating special exhibits.
Day trip · about 70 km from Milwaukee. Two miles of Lake Michigan beach, sand dunes, pine woods, a nature center, and camping at this Wisconsin state park near Sheboygan.
Three beehive-shaped glass domes housing a tropical rainforest, a desert and seasonal floral shows.
Natural and human history museum with dinosaur halls, a walk-through Streets of Old Milwaukee, a butterfly vivarium and planetarium.
Formal gardens in Whitnall Park with rose, rock, herb and perennial gardens and a bog walk.
Three-mile walkway along both banks of the Milwaukee River through downtown and the Third Ward.
185-acre nature preserve on the Lake Michigan bluffs with forest trails, an observation tower and live birds of prey.
a.l: 1111 E Brown Deer Rd, Bayside, WI 53217

a.d: Urban state park on a man-made island on Milwaukee's lakefront, with paved trails, prairie and skyline views.
Beautiful architectural terrace path overlooking Lake Monona.
A free-admission, AZA-accredited zoo in Madison with polar bears, lions, giraffes, and a carousel — one of the few free zoos left in the country.

The Wisconsin State Capitol, completed in 1917, houses both chambers of the Wisconsin Legislature and the Wisconsin Supreme Court. It is open to the public seven days a week, and guided tours are free. Inside are mosaics, towering marble columns and artwork.
16 acres of themed outdoor gardens plus the Bolz Conservatory's tropical plants, free-flying birds, and a gilded Thai pavilion — a calm, beautiful family outing.

The eccentric Alex Jordan-built attraction near Spring Green, Wisconsin, featuring the glass-walled Infinity Room extending 218 feet over the valley, a large one-of-a-kind carousel, and miles of oddball exhibits.
1,200-acre university arboretum with restored prairies, woodlands, gardens and 17 miles of trails on Lake Wingra.
Children's museum off Capitol Square with three floors of hands-on exhibits and a rooftop garden with animals.
Free museum on Capitol Square about Wisconsin's veterans from the Civil War to today, with aircraft and artifacts.
Mile-long wooded peninsula jutting into Lake Mendota with a walking path, fire circles and views back to the Madison skyline.
Day trip · about 35 km from Madison. National Natural Landmark limestone cave west of Madison with guided tours past stalactites, stalagmites and flowstone.
a.l: 2975 Cave of the Mounds Rd, Blue Mounds, WI 53517

a.d: 2.5-acre UW–Madison teaching garden with themed gardens around an 1896 Victorian house; free and open dawn to dusk.
Spectacular towering sandstone rock cliffs lining the Wisconsin River.
Wisconsin's most-visited state park, with 500-foot quartzite bluffs overlooking a 360-acre lake, nearly 30 miles of hiking trails, sandy swimming beaches, lakeshore picnic areas and paddling.
America's largest outdoor waterpark in Wisconsin Dells, featuring 50+ water slides, wave pools, lazy rivers, and family-friendly attractions. Open seasonally.
State park around a calm, sandstone-walled lake just south of the Dells, with canoe and kayak rentals and wooded trails.
Conservation center that is home to all 15 of the world's crane species, with naturalistic exhibits and prairie trails.
a.l: E11376 Shady Lane Rd, Baraboo, WI 53913

a.d: Outdoor railroad museum with restored steam-era trains and a seven-mile round-trip ride through the Baraboo River valley.
a.l: E8948 Museum Rd, North Freedom, WI 53951

a.d: Small state park in a pine-shaded sandstone gorge carved by the ancient Wisconsin River, with a one-mile nature trail.
State historic site in the 1875 studio of photographer H.H. Bennett, whose pictures of the Dells' rock formations made the area famous.
Day trip · about 35 km from Wisconsin Dells. Park around Wisconsin's largest natural sandstone arch, reached by a short wooded hiking trail.

a.n: Grand Teton National Park Scenic Loop
a.d: Stunning craggy snow-draped peak range reflecting off Jenny and Jackson lakes.
A charming public plaza flanked by four massive arches built entirely from shed elk antlers.
Jagged peaks, moose and bear watching, Jenny Lake boat rides, and Junior Ranger programs a short drive from Jackson.

Day trip · about 130 km from Jackson Hole. Yellowstone, the first national park, is renowned for its hydrothermal features (including Old Faithful) and abundant wildlife. The park spans parts of Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho.
Winter home to thousands of elk right at Jackson's edge, with horse-drawn sleigh rides through the herds in winter.
The "Big Red Box" climbs 4,139 vertical feet in 12 minutes to the top of Rendezvous Mountain for sweeping views of the Tetons and the valley.
Stone museum built into a butte overlooking the National Elk Refuge, with wildlife paintings and a hillside trail of large animal sculptures.
In-town ski hill whose gondola rides to a summit observatory and viewpoints over Jackson, with an alpine coaster and trails in season.
1890s homesteading settlement with the famous T.A. Moulton Barn framed by the Teton Range.
a.l: Antelope Flats Rd, Grand Teton National Park, WY 83012

a.d: Unbelievably massive, brilliant rainbow-colored geothermal hot springs.

a.n: Buffalo Bill Center of the West
a.d: Day trip · about 120 km from Yellowstone. Five museums under one roof (Buffalo Bill, Plains Indians, Western art, firearms, natural history) with two-day admission.
20-mile yellow-and-orange canyon carved by the Yellowstone River, with the 308-foot Lower Falls seen from rim viewpoints like Artist Point and Lookout Point.
a.l: Canyon Village, Yellowstone National Park, WY 82190

a.d: Travertine terraces built by hot springs into stepped white and orange cascades, explored on boardwalks near park headquarters; elk often graze the lawns.
a.l: Mammoth Hot Springs, Yellowstone National Park, WY 82190

a.d: Broad valley in Yellowstone's northeast called the "Serengeti of North America," home to bison herds, wolves, pronghorn and bears.
a.l: Northeast Entrance Rd, Yellowstone National Park, WY

a.d: Boardwalk loop of hot springs and geysers on the shore of Yellowstone Lake, including pools and cones right at the water's edge.
a.l: West Thumb, Yellowstone National Park, WY 82190

a.d: Day trip · about 50 km from Yellowstone. Nonprofit wildlife park where rescued grizzly bears and wolf packs that cannot live in the wild are seen up close, with raptor programs.
a.l: 201 S Canyon St, West Yellowstone, MT 59758

a.d: Day trip · about 70 km from Yellowstone. Stone arch at Yellowstone's North Entrance, dedicated in 1903, inscribed "For the Benefit and Enjoyment of the People."
An 11-mile paved multi-use trail along Anchorage's coast, used for walking, running, biking, rollerblading, and in winter cross-country skiing, open 24/7 year-round.
A renowned cultural center celebrating the traditions, songs, and historical dwellings of Alaska’s Indigenous peoples.
Alaska's largest museum, covering Alaska Native cultures, history, science and the Arctic, with a hands-on discovery center for kids and a planetarium.
a.l: Anchorage Museum, C Street, downtown Anchorage, AK 99501

a.d: Day trip · about 65 km from Anchorage. Drive-through and walking sanctuary for orphaned and injured Alaska animals, including brown and black bears, moose, wood bison, musk oxen and elk.
Alaska's most-climbed peak, a steep 3-mile round trip in Chugach State Park from the Glen Alps trailhead to a flat summit with views of Anchorage and Denali.
a.l: Glen Alps Trailhead, Chugach State Park, Anchorage, AK

a.d: Coastal park where the 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake slid a neighborhood into the inlet, with interpretive signs, trails through the slide area and views of Denali.
a.l: Earthquake Park, W Northern Lights Blvd, Anchorage, AK 99517

a.d: Museum on Lake Hood, the world's busiest seaplane base, with restored bush planes, hangars and a viewing area for floatplane takeoffs.
Day trip · about 25 km from Anchorage. Rocky pullout on the scenic Seward Highway along Turnagain Arm, known for views of the bore tide, mountains and, in season, beluga whales.
a.l: Beluga Point Viewpoint, Seward Hwy, Anchorage, AK

a.d: Boardwalk over a wetland refuge at the south edge of Anchorage for watching nesting waterfowl, bald eagles, salmon and occasionally moose.
a.l: Potter Marsh boardwalk, Seward Hwy, Anchorage, AK 99516

a.d: Day trip · about 45 km from Anchorage. Glacier-fed turquoise lake in Chugach State Park with a lakeside trail for biking and walking, kayaking and mountain views.
a.l: Eklutna Lake Rd, Chugach State Park, AK 99577

a.d: A spectacular 13-mile-long river of ice winding into Mendenhall Lake, featuring the roaring Nugget Falls trail.
Rises 1,800 feet through lush rainforest to mountain-top vistas of the Gastineau Channel.
A narrow, glacier-carved fjord in the Tongass National Forest south of Juneau, within the Tracy Arm-Fords Terror Wilderness, known for waterfalls, floating ice, wildlife, and the Sawyer Glaciers.
State museum of Alaska history, Native cultures and natural history in the modern Andrew P. Kashevaroff building.
Botanical garden in the Tongass rainforest famous for "flower towers," upside-down tree trunks planted with flowers, with guided cart rides up the mountainside.
Working salmon hatchery with a fish ladder where returning salmon climb in late summer, plus aquariums of Southeast Alaska sea life.
Historic compressor building of the Alaska-Juneau gold mine in Gold Creek basin, with original machinery, mining tools and a 3D map of the tunnels.
a.l: Last Chance Mining Museum, Basin Rd, Juneau, AK 99801

a.d: Juneau's first road, now a trail up Gold Creek valley past waterfalls, old mine ruins and cool-air mine shafts, starting minutes from downtown.
a.l: Perseverance Trailhead, end of Basin Rd, Juneau, AK 99801

a.d: Hot springs resort about 60 miles east of Fairbanks with an outdoor geothermal mineral-water lake (Rock Lake), an indoor pool, Northern Lights viewing, and guided tours of the Aurora Ice Museum.

A 44-acre historical park in Fairbanks, originally known as Alaskaland and later renamed Pioneer Park. It features museums and exhibits on early Alaskan pioneer life, including a gold rush-era mining display and a preserved Sternwheeler riverboat (the SS Nenana).

a.n: University of Alaska Museum of the North
a.d: Striking white museum on the UAF campus with Alaska's natural and cultural history, a famous mummified steppe bison and gold collections.
Three-hour sternwheeler cruise on the Chena and Tanana rivers with a bush-pilot demonstration, sled-dog kennel stop and a re-created Athabascan village.
Former dairy farm turned refuge in town, with trails and boardwalks where sandhill cranes and geese gather in spring and fall, and a historic farmhouse visitor center.

a.n: Kenai Fjords National Park Glacier Cruise
a.d: Board a scenic vessel to witness massive calving glaciers crash into the sea and spot wild seals, puffins, and humpbacks.
An accessible walking trail that leads right to the edge of a towering, brilliant blue glacial flow.
Public aquarium and marine research center on Resurrection Bay with Steller sea lions, harbor seals, puffins and a touch tank.
Coastal park south of Seward with beach hikes (timed with low tide) and the WWII Fort McGilvray bunkers on a headland above Resurrection Bay.
a.l: Caines Head SRA, south of Seward on Resurrection Bay (coastal trail from the Lowell Point area, or by boat)

a.d: Mile-long shoreline park and path along Resurrection Bay with mountain views, interpretive signs and frequent sea otter sightings.
An aerial tramway at Alyeska Resort that glides up the mountain to an observation deck at 2,300 feet, offering panoramic views of surrounding peaks and glaciers.
A short, well-marked trail, about 0.4 to 0.5 mile round trip, through temperate rainforest to a small waterfall and pool near Alyeska Resort in Girdwood.
Historic 1890s gold mine with original buildings where visitors pan for gold in Crow Creek.
Boardwalk and forest trail through temperate rainforest from Alyeska to Winner Creek Gorge, where the creek rushes through a narrow canyon.
a.l: Winner Creek trailhead near Alyeska Resort, Girdwood, AK 99587

a.d: Forest Service visitor center on Portage Lake with exhibits on glaciers and views of icebergs and Portage Glacier's valley.
a.l: Begich, Boggs Visitor Center, Portage Lake, Chugach National Forest, AK (mailing: 145 Forest Station Rd, Girdwood)

a.d: Soar past sheer granite faces of Denali and land on a massive active glacier to step onto pristine snow fields.
Stroll along gravel bars at the confluence of the Talkeetna, Chulitna, and Susitna Rivers, with panoramic views of Denali and the Alaska Range.

a.n: Denali State Park (Byers Lake & K'esugi Ridge)
a.d: Day trip · about 45 km from Talkeetna. Large state park beside the Parks Highway with lake and ridge trails and some of the best roadside views of Denali, at viewpoints like Denali View South (Mile 135.2).
a.l: Byers Lake, Mile 147 Parks Hwy, Denali State Park, AK

a.d: A 2-mile riverside walking loop following the Savage River through a canyon between Mount Margaret and Healy Ridge in Denali National Park and Preserve, featuring subalpine tundra flora.
Take the national park transit bus into deep pristine wilderness to search for moose, caribou, grizzly bears, and wolves.
The only sled-dog kennels in a U.S. national park, where rangers' working huskies live; visitors meet the dogs and, in summer, watch sled demonstrations.
a.l: Park Headquarters on Denali Park Rd, a short drive/shuttle from Denali Visitor Center, AK 99755

a.d: Easy 3-mile loop down to an oxbow lake along the Nenana River, a good spot to see beavers and moose near the park entrance.
a.l: Horseshoe Lake trailhead near Denali Visitor Center, Denali National Park, AK

a.d: Steep 5-mile round-trip climb from the park entrance area to a ridge overlook of the Nenana River valley and the Alaska Range.
a.l: Trailhead near Denali Visitor Center, Denali National Park, AK

a.d: A narrow 4.5-mile strip of land extending into Kachemak Bay, known for fishing, beachcombing, shops, restaurants and a working boat harbor, with a paved 4-mile walking and biking path.

a.n: Kachemak Bay State Park Water Taxi Tour
a.d: Take a brief water taxi over pristine waters to explore rugged coastlines, towering glaciers, and mossy pine hiking trails.
Visitor center of the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge with seabird-colony exhibits and trails to Bishop's Beach through wetlands.
Museum of Kachemak Bay's natural history and people, with marine aquariums, a historic homestead cabin and forest trails.
Wide, driftwood-strewn beach in town facing Kachemak Bay and the glaciated Kenai Mountains, great for tidepooling at low tide.
Board an ultra-smooth high-speed catamaran to view twenty-six spectacular active glaciers calving into the deep waters of Prince William Sound.
A scenic 2-mile alpine hike that crosses Portage Pass, offering sweeping views of Portage Glacier and Lake. Suitable for a range of hikers, with a steeper initial climb.
North America's longest highway tunnel at 2.5 miles, a one-lane passage shared on a timed schedule by cars and Alaska Railroad trains.
Former Army barracks where nearly the whole town lives under one 14-story roof, with the post office, police and shops inside; seen from outside, it's a striking piece of Cold War history.
Deep fjord at Whittier's harbor framed by hanging glaciers and waterfalls, the starting point for Prince William Sound cruises.

State recreation site in Thompson Pass, about 28 miles north of Valdez on the Richardson Highway. A short paved, wheelchair-accessible trail leads to a viewing platform overlooking Worthington Glacier, often called one of Alaska's most accessible glaciers. Open until closed by winter snow.
Drive through a breathtakingly narrow sheer canyon flanked by towering waterfalls like Horsetail Falls and Bridal Veil Falls.
Museum of Valdez history, from the gold-rush trail and the 1964 earthquake that destroyed the old town to the Trans-Alaska Pipeline terminal, with an 1886 hand-pumped fire engine.
A historic wooden boardwalk built on stilts over Creek Street stream, now home to cozy local art galleries and gift shops.

a.n: Misty Fjords National Monument Floatplane Tour
a.d: Floatplane flightseeing tours from Ketchikan over Misty Fjords National Monument, with views of granite cliffs rising about 3,000 feet from the fjords, waterfalls and lakes. Tours run about 1-2 hours, and some include a landing stopover.
Steep rainforest trail starting near downtown that climbs to alpine views over Ketchikan, the Tongass Narrows and surrounding islands.
A narrow-gauge vintage rail excursion from Skagway that travels through dramatic mountain scenery, passing canyon gorges, waterfalls, and tunnels along the historic White Pass route.

a.n: Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park
a.d: National historical park preserving the history of the 1897-98 Klondike Gold Rush. In Skagway it includes over 20 historic buildings, four of them museums. The visitor center at 2nd Ave and Broadway has old photos, films and ranger talks.
Site of the vanished 1897 boomtown at the start of the Chilkoot Trail, with tide flats, ruins of the old wharf and the first easy miles of the gold-rush trail.
a.l: Dyea, Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park (via Dyea Rd from Skagway), AK 99840

a.d: Easy 2-mile loop from town over the Skagway River footbridge to rocky lookouts and a quiet cove on Taiya Inlet.
a.l: Yakutania Point trail (across the footbridge from downtown), Skagway, AK 99840

a.d: Community museum in the 1899 granite McCabe College building, with gold-rush artifacts, Tlingit items and stories of Skagway's boom years.

a.n: Sitka National Historical Park Totem Walk
a.d: Stroll scenic loop trails under giant moss-draped spruce trees, decorated with majestic hand-carved Haida and Tlingit totem poles.
Rescue center for orphaned brown and black bear cubs, housed in former pulp-mill clarifier tanks, with viewing platforms over the habitats.

a.n: Castle Hill (Baranof Castle State Historic Site)
a.d: Hilltop site where Alaska was formally transferred from Russia to the United States in 1867, with a short ramp, cannons and views over Sitka Sound.
a.l: Castle Hill, Harbor Way, Sitka, AK 99835

a.d: Park in Washington, DC with the Washington Monument and memorials to Lincoln, MLK, FDR, WWII and Vietnam veterans, stretching between the Capitol and Lincoln Memorial.
Smithsonian museum on the National Mall with the Wright Flyer, the Apollo 11 command module and galleries of historic aircraft and spacecraft.

Day trip · about 35 km from Washington. The Air and Space Museum's huge hangar near Dulles Airport, displaying the Space Shuttle Discovery, an SR-71 Blackbird and the Enola Gay, with an observation tower.

t: Hotel Zone Public Transit (Buses vs Taxis): Public city buses (routes R-1 and R-2) run up and down Blvd. Kukulcán 24 hours a day for only ~MX$12 in cash. They are safe, air-conditioned, frequent, and significantly more affordable than private hotel taxis for traveling between downtown, Punta Cancún, and southern hotel zone beaches.

Cancun Airport (CUN) Terminal 3 Logistics: The Priority Pass lounge in Terminal 3 (The Lounge) is landside, before the security checkpoint, so visit it before going through security. Note that Mexico does not conduct exit passport control checks when departing on international flights.

Airport Taxi Union Rates: Taxis from Punta Cancun or the Hotel Zone to Cancun Airport Terminal 3 charge steep union-regulated prices (~MX$650 / $38 USD for a <30-minute ride). ADO express buses from downtown Cancun offer a budget alternative for solo travelers.

Punta Cancún Stroll & Luggage Drop: If you have a late afternoon or evening departure, you can arrange luggage drop-off at Chabad of Cancun, spend a relaxing afternoon walking around Punta Cancún and enjoying an early dinner at Ember Kosher, and take a 25-minute taxi directly to CUN Airport.

Punta Cancún Access & Beach Conditions: Punta Cancún (around kilometer 9–9.5) marks the natural bend where the coastline transitions from quiet, wave-protected north-facing waters (Playa Caracol) to breezy eastern surf beaches (Playa Gaviota Azul). The scenic red-and-white Punta Cancún Lighthouse can be reached via a pleasant seaside walk starting from Playa Caracol.

Shabbat & Kosher Meal Planning: Shabbat meal packages should be reserved early in the week with Chabad of Cancun at Plaza Kukulcán (km 13). If staying in northern Punta Cancún resorts, prepare for a ~40-minute walk south along the pedestrian sidewalk or reserve accommodations located within immediate walking distance of Plaza Kukulcán.

a.d: World-renowned marine sanctuary along the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, celebrated for towering coral pinnacles, deep swim-through caves, and crystal-clear underwater visibility.

a.d: Adventure park inside Cozumel's National Reef Marine Park with a beach, a lagoon, reef snorkeling and scuba diving, a tropical garden, prehispanic replicas, a Mayan hut and a kids' playground. Some activities, such as dolphin swims, cost extra.

a.d: Protected ecological reserve at Cozumel's southern tip, home to the historic Celarain lighthouse, crocodile observation towers on Colombia Lagoon, and white-sand beaches.
a.l: Carretera Costera Sur Km 30, 77600 Cozumel, Q.R., Mexico

a.d: Lush private ecological reserve nestled in Cozumel’s interior jungle along Camino a Villa Maya, dedicated to rainforest conservation, native biodiversity, and peaceful nature walks.
a.l: Camino a Villa Maya Km 2, San Gervasio, 77660 San Miguel de Cozumel, Q.R., Mexico

a.d: Ancient pre-Columbian Mayan archaeological site on Cozumel, long considered a pilgrimage center dedicated to the goddess Ixchel, with several Mayan structures to explore amid island wildlife.

Central waterfront plaza and gathering point in downtown San Miguel de Cozumel, steps from the ferry terminal, with a historic clock tower, a shaded gazebo, a fountain, benches and the colorful COZUMEL sign, surrounded by shops, cafés and restaurants.
a.l: C. 1 Sur 58, Centro, 77668 Cozumel, Q.R., Mexico

a.d: Spacious civic park in Cozumel with a monument to independence figure Andrés Quintana Roo, open-air event pavilions, tree-lined walking areas, spaces where children play, and lively evening gatherings with live music and local island atmosphere.

a.n: Museo de la Isla de Cozumel

a.l: Av. Rafael E. Melgar, between Calles 4 & 6 Norte, San Miguel de Cozumel, Q.R., Mexico

a.d: Wild, undeveloped windward coast reached on the island's perimeter road, with rocky points, crashing surf and lookouts such as El Mirador.
a.l: Carretera Costera Oriente, Punta Morena, Cozumel, Q.R., Mexico

t: Airport Arrival & Shared Shuttles: When arriving at Cozumel International Airport (CZM), skip the expensive private airport taxis and buy a ticket for the shared shuttle at the counter inside the terminal for the quick ride to Chabad of Cozumel or downtown hotels.

Chabad Hospitality & Luggage Drop: Chabad of Cozumel is exceptionally welcoming, staffed by energetic bochurim, and happily accommodates luggage storage for travelers needing a safe place for bags before checking in or heading on a catamaran excursion.

Climate & Passing Showers: Stepping off flights from dry Mexico City into Cozumel brings an immediate wave of tropical Caribbean humidity. Mid-afternoon rain showers occur frequently but typically clear within 10 to 15 minutes.

Interior Transportation: When heading into Cozumel’s interior to visit Villa Maya or San Gervasio ruins, arrange a taxi driver in advance to wait for you or agree on a scheduled return pickup, as cell reception can be spotty and return cabs are rarely available on the highway.

Interior Access Road Closures: The interior transversal roads and connecting unpaved paths leading to inland reserves like Villa Maya and San Gervasio can occasionally close without notice due to private land maintenance, municipal forestry works, or heavy rainfall. Confirm road conditions with your hotel concierge or local drivers prior to departure.

Ferry Logistics from Playa del Carmen: Passenger ferries between Playa del Carmen and San Miguel de Cozumel depart hourly from morning until night, operated alternately by Ultramar and Winjet. Purchase one-way tickets instead of round-trips so you can board whichever ferry leaves next on your return rather than waiting an extra hour for your original company.

Reef-Safe Sunscreen Rule: Cozumel Reefs National Park (Palancar, Colombia), Chankanaab and most cenotes and eco-parks allow only biodegradable (reef-safe) sunscreen. Bring biodegradable sunscreen or wear UV-protective rashguards.

t: Communal Shabbat Atmosphere at Chabad: Chabad of Playa del Carmen hosts legendary Friday night dinners drawing 100+ Jewish travelers from around the globe, with enthusiastic singing, dancing, and abundant multi-course meals. Shabbat day lunch is equally welcoming and hearty.

Public Beach Access by Federal Law: In Playa del Carmen and across Mexico, all ocean beaches are legally public property. Even when beachfront resorts or beach clubs occupy the shoreline, public pedestrian access to and along the sand cannot be restricted or blocked.

Hilula Bakery for Shabbat Provisions: Located on Avenida 20 between Calle 6 and Calle 8, Hilula Bakery is the go-to spot for purchasing fresh Shabbat challah, babka, and baked goods prior to candle lighting.

ADO Alterna Express Bus to Cancun: Skip expensive long-distance taxis and head to the Playa del Carmen Alterna terminal (Av. 20 and Calle 12). Departures to Cancun run every 10 to 20 minutes for about MX$124 (ADO quotes vary by departure). The buses are clean, prompt, and arrive at Cancun Central Bus Station in about 1 hour and 5 minutes.

Excursion Planning on Avenida 5: When booking day excursions (Tulum ruins, cenotes, or the Punta Laguna monkey reserve) from Quinta Avenida kiosks, note that tours can sell out or close early during peak travel seasons and winter breaks. Book well in advance.

Playa del Carmen Taxi Rules & Union Rates: Uber is approved in Quintana Roo, but taxis are still the most common option. The local taxi union sets fixed zone rates. Always agree on the exact total fare with the driver before getting in, especially for trips outside the downtown grid.

Cozumel Ferry Logistics: Passenger ferries to Cozumel depart directly from the downtown maritime terminal by Parque Los Fundadores every hour on the hour. Because two distinct ferry companies (Ultramar and Winjet) alternate hourly departures, buy one-way tickets to keep your return schedule completely flexible.

Cenote Environmental Preservation: All visitors are required to take a cleansing shower before entering natural cenote pools. Chemical sunscreens, bug sprays, and body lotions are strictly prohibited to preserve the sensitive underground Mayan aquifer.

t: Pacific Ocean vs. Sea of Cortez Swimmability: Most open Pacific-facing beaches in Cabo have treacherous shorebreaks and severe undertows where swimming is strictly prohibited. Stick to designated swimmable beaches like Playa El Médano, Chileno Bay, and Santa Maria Beach.

Whale Watching Timing: Peak humpback and gray whale migration occurs between mid-December and mid-April. Early morning boat departures (8:00 AM–9:30 AM) offer the calmest sea surface and easiest whale spotting.

Kosher Meal Pre-Coordination Rule: Resort kosher dining is strictly NOT available on-demand at check-in. Coordinate with Rabbi Benny at Chabad of Cabo San Lucas at least 1–2 weeks prior to arrival to schedule catering and a mashgiach.

Corridor Transportation: The Tourist Corridor between Cabo San Lucas and San José del Cabo spans 20 miles. Rental cars or pre-arranged private transfers are far more cost-effective than relying on individual hotel taxi dispatches, which have steep flat union rates.

Shabbat Logistics in Los Cabos: Chabad is located in the Pedregal district of Cabo San Lucas. If staying out along the corridor (e.g. Solaz or Zadún), arrange Shabbat delivery boxes in advance as walking to shul from the corridor is not feasible.

t: Rideshare App Comparison (DiDi vs Uber): Download DiDi before arriving in Mexico City. DiDi has extensive driver availability and is routinely 30–40% cheaper than Uber. If a DiDi driver’s final fare increases after the trip, tap the help button in the app to request an immediate refund back to the initial quote.

High-Altitude Dry Climate & Lip Care: Mexico City sits at an elevation of 7,350 feet (2,240m). The mountain air is notably dry and combined with urban smog can cause dry, chapped, or swollen lips. Keep ChapStick/lip balm on hand and drink plenty of bottled water (tap water is not potable).

Safety & Visible Police Presence: Mexico City maintains a heavy, reassuring tourist police presence across Polanco, Reforma, Centro Histórico, Roma, and Condesa. Daytime and early evening walking along main avenues is comfortable and safe.
MEX Airport Terminal 2 Departures: Arrive at least 2 hours before domestic flights.

Chapultepec Castle & Park Logistics: Chapultepec Castle is North America’s only royal-inhabited castle (Emperor Maximilian I and Empress Carlota). Note that public restrooms within the surrounding Bosque de Chapultepec park charge a small cash entry fee (~MX$5 coins required). The uphill walk takes 10–15 minutes.

Xochimilco Canal Booking at Embarcadero Nativitas: Head to Embarcadero Nuevo Nativitas (the largest dock). Trajinera boat rentals have an official rate set by the Xochimilco borough of MX$750 per hour for the whole boat (2025), not per person. Confirm duration and price before boarding.
KMD Kosher Certification: The main kosher certifier in Mexico City is KMD (Kashrut Maguen David), Horacio 1008, Polanco. Check kosher.com.mx for current certified products and establishments.

t: January Yeshivah Week Surge Warning: Puerto Rico’s Jewish infrastructure experiences heavy demand during the annual two-week January Yeshivah Week period. Chabad Shabbat meals frequently sell out completely weeks in advance (they often erect an outdoor overflow tent), and OMRKT can have lines down the block with hour-plus waits or run out of food by late evening. If visiting in January, reserve Chabad Shabbat meals well ahead of time, arrive early at OMRKT, or bring hotel cooking appliances.

Westchester (HPN) Flight Alternative: For travelers originating in Monsey, Rockland County, Westchester, or northern NJ, JetBlue flights from Westchester County Airport (HPN) to SJU offer a serene, relaxed alternative to JFK or Newark, featuring swift security lines and hassle-free boarding.

La Posita de Piñones Natural Tidal Lagoon: Located just 5-10 minutes east of Isla Verde. While the main Piñones road consists of non-kosher street kiosks, Terraplén La Posita de Piñones is an absolute hidden paradise: an ancient offshore barrier reef breaks violent ocean waves, creating a calm, shallow, crystal-clear natural swimming pool where water trickles gently over rocks. Ideal for relaxed swimming, hunting shells, and strolling the shaded oceanfront boardwalk.

El Yunque Natural Waterslides (Las Paylas / Charco Frío): For active adventurers, guided trips lead through bamboo groves to natural granite waterslides, river rope swings, and cliff jumps. Don’t worry if you didn’t pack water shoes—a local stand right at the mucky parking lot entrance sells inexpensive water shoes, waterproof phone pouches, and river gear directly on-site.

Travel Heating Devices (HotLogic Mini & Panini Grills): Packing a compact HotLogic mini portable oven allows slow, safe heating of frozen double-wrapped kosher meals (e.g. MealMart) right in your hotel room over several hours without burning or kitchen hassles. A compact panini press / sandwich grill is also ideal for warming par-baked baguettes, pizza bagels, and grilled cheese.

SJU Airport Departure USDA Agricultural Scan: When departing SJU for the US mainland, all checked luggage and carry-on bags must pass through a mandatory USDA agricultural inspection scanner before entering airline check-in lines or TSA security checkpoints. Allow an extra 15-20 minutes at the airport for this routine scan.

Old San Juan Museum Schedules & Audio Tours: Most historic museums in Old San Juan are closed on Mondays and Tuesdays (operating Wednesday through Sunday). Self-guided GPS audio apps (like Action Tour Guides) are an excellent fallback, providing detailed historical narration walking from the cruise docks past Castillo San Cristóbal, El Morro, and the colorful La Perla seaside enclave.

The Perfect Puerto Rico Split-Stay: For frum travelers, a winning itinerary is spending Thursday to Sunday in Isla Verde (Fairmont El San Juan, Residence Inn, or Hampton Inn), near the eruv (confirm with Chabad whether your hotel is inside it) and a short stroll to Chabad for Shabbat prayers and community dinners. On Sunday, transition east to The St. Regis Bahia Beach in Río Grande for serene rainforest luxury, tranquil beach pools, and immediate access to El Yunque and eastern excursions.

El Yunque Next-Day Ticket Drop: If vehicle passes or trail permits appear sold out weeks in advance on recreation.gov, don’t panic: the US Forest Service releases a major batch of next-day tickets every morning at 8:00 AM AST the day prior to entry. Set an alarm to snag your reservation easily.

Mainland Bio Bay (Laguna Grande / Fajardo) vs. Vieques (Mosquito Bay): Travelers should weigh expectations carefully. While Laguna Grande in Fajardo is an easy drive from San Juan, the kayak tour requires navigating narrow mangrove grass channels against stiff currents on the paddle back, mosquitoes can be fierce, and water glow is often very dim. For the true bucket-list electric-blue glow, make the trip to Mosquito Bay in Vieques (the world’s brightest biobay) and time it during the moonless nights of Rosh Chodesh.

Balcony Prep & Sunset Grilling: If staying at beachfront properties like Fairmont El San Juan, rooms feature balconies suitable for well-ventilated travel cooking with compact electric appliances. Additionally, public coastal parks around San Juan offer breathtaking sunset spots for grilling dinners with portable disposable grills.

SJU Airport Arrivals & Taxi Hack: When multiple flights land simultaneously at SJU, Uber activates surge pricing (climbing from $8 to $35), while curbside taxi drivers often solicit $25. Walk across to the official airport parking garage taxi stand where standard regulated fares to Isla Verde run ~$16. When returning off-peak to SJU, an Uber can cost as little as $4.

TSA & Frozen Kosher Liquids: You can pack frozen Cholov Yisroel milk bottles and cheeses through TSA security checkpoints without checking bags, provided they are frozen solid when passing the scanner. Using a small personal-item cooler bag alongside backpacks allows a seamless carry-on trip.

Supermarket Provisions & Betty Crocker Cooking: Pueblo Supermarket in Isla Verde is within easy walking distance of the Residence Inn and Chabad, stocking kosher-certified wraps, eggs, pizza sauce, smoked salmon, pareve cookies, ices, and potatoes. Bringing a mini-Betty Crocker electric skillet/pizza maker allows quick hotel-room prep of hot meals, grilled wraps, and potato kugel.

Local Canned Sodas & Kashrus Vigilance: Unlike US mainland stores where brands like Schweppes or Gatorade are universally certified, local Puerto Rican bottling plants produce versions without kosher certification logos. Always check the physical can/bottle for a reliable kosher symbol before purchasing.

Old San Juan Walking & Parking Logistics: Municipal parking lots (e.g. near the port or Paseo Covadonga) cost only ~$5 for the day. Explore early in the morning or late in the afternoon, as midday Caribbean sun and humidity can be intense. Bacardi Rum Factory tours cost ~$40/person and require travel across the bay—skippable unless you are a committed rum aficionado.

El Yunque National Forest Practicalities: The drive is ~45 minutes east of San Juan. Drive directly onto Highway PR-191 to access Yokahú Tower, Mount Britton, and Juan Diego Falls. Caution: Parking is strictly enforced in designated bays only; rangers issue steep $150 tickets for parking on non-designated road shoulders. The trail climb behind Juan Diego Falls can be extremely slick and dangerous when wet. Applying mosquito patches or repellent ensures a completely bug-free rainforest hike.

t: Shabbat & Family Travel in Aruba: Chabad of Aruba hosts welcoming Shabbat dinners, uplifting tefilos, festive Friday night meals, and community Havdalah. Bocobay Porta al Sole Condos (right around the corner) feature private rooftop terraces ideal for relaxing family meals.

Shabbat in Aruba: Make advance reservations for Friday night dinner at Piccolo Italian Steakhouse (piccoloaruba.com) or book communal Shabbat meals and "Shabbat-in-a-Bag" takeout with Chabad of Aruba (jewisharuba.com).
Walking to Chabad: Bocobay Porta al Sole is a 2-minute stroll to Chabad on Salina Cerca. High-rise hotels on Palm Beach (Hyatt Regency, Marriott, Ritz-Carlton) are a flat 15-20 minute walk.
Best Snorkeling & Sunsets: Head to Tres Trapi Beach for natural limestone carved steps, sea turtles, and jaw-dropping golden hour sunsets, and Arashi Beach for shallow family-friendly fish feeding.
Family Attractions: Don't miss the Aruba Butterfly Farm near Palm Beach and the Atlantis Submarine dive for an unforgettable live undersea "aquarium" experience.

Self-Catering & Bringing Food: For travelers bringing home-cooked meals, boutique hotels like Ocean Z in Malmok are exceptionally kosher-friendly—offering double-wrapped food warming, large refrigerators, and raw uncut produce/eggs. Packing a travel mini-griddle or electric pan makes hot breakfasts (pancakes, omelets) effortless.
Sun & Wind: Aruba's pleasant trade winds mask strong UV radiation (12°N latitude). Use broad-spectrum reef-safe sunscreen and stay hydrated.

State park with beaches, trails, pier fishing, tennis, golf, and a zip line above the dunes.
67.5 acres of beautiful gardens with over 12,000 different plants.
Museum documenting the Civil Rights Movement in Birmingham.
Home to the world's largest cast-iron statue with panoramic city views.
An 11-mile paved multi-use trail along Anchorage's coast, used for walking, running, biking, rollerblading, and in winter cross-country skiing, open 24/7 year-round.
A renowned cultural center celebrating the traditions, songs, and historical dwellings of Alaska’s Indigenous peoples.
Alaska's largest museum, covering Alaska Native cultures, history, science and the Arctic, with a hands-on discovery center for kids and a planetarium.
a.l: Anchorage Museum, C Street, downtown Anchorage, AK 99501

a.d: Day trip · about 65 km from Anchorage. Drive-through and walking sanctuary for orphaned and injured Alaska animals, including brown and black bears, moose, wood bison, musk oxen and elk.
Alaska's most-climbed peak, a steep 3-mile round trip in Chugach State Park from the Glen Alps trailhead to a flat summit with views of Anchorage and Denali.
a.l: Glen Alps Trailhead, Chugach State Park, Anchorage, AK

a.d: Coastal park where the 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake slid a neighborhood into the inlet, with interpretive signs, trails through the slide area and views of Denali.
a.l: Earthquake Park, W Northern Lights Blvd, Anchorage, AK 99517

a.d: Museum on Lake Hood, the world's busiest seaplane base, with restored bush planes, hangars and a viewing area for floatplane takeoffs.
Day trip · about 25 km from Anchorage. Rocky pullout on the scenic Seward Highway along Turnagain Arm, known for views of the bore tide, mountains and, in season, beluga whales.
a.l: Beluga Point Viewpoint, Seward Hwy, Anchorage, AK

a.d: Boardwalk over a wetland refuge at the south edge of Anchorage for watching nesting waterfowl, bald eagles, salmon and occasionally moose.
a.l: Potter Marsh boardwalk, Seward Hwy, Anchorage, AK 99516

a.d: Day trip · about 45 km from Anchorage. Glacier-fed turquoise lake in Chugach State Park with a lakeside trail for biking and walking, kayaking and mountain views.
a.l: Eklutna Lake Rd, Chugach State Park, AK 99577

a.d: A 2-mile riverside walking loop following the Savage River through a canyon between Mount Margaret and Healy Ridge in Denali National Park and Preserve, featuring subalpine tundra flora.
Take the national park transit bus into deep pristine wilderness to search for moose, caribou, grizzly bears, and wolves.
140 acres of desert trails with 50,000 plants, themed gardens, and seasonal events like the butterfly pavilion and holiday luminarias.
One of the country's largest nonprofit zoos: over 3,000 animals on themed trails, giraffe feeding, a stingray touch tank, and camel rides.
Internationally renowned museum of American Indian art, from Hopi katsina dolls to contemporary Native works, with family programs and events.

Hands-on children's museum in the historic Monroe School Building in downtown Phoenix, with more than 300 play experiences across three floors, including a climber, an art studio and a children's garden.
Museum displaying thousands of musical instruments from about 200 countries, with headphone audio-video guides and a hands-on Experience Gallery.
Hands-on science museum in downtown Phoenix's Heritage and Science Park with interactive galleries and a planetarium.
Desert park of red sandstone buttes on the Phoenix-Tempe border, with the short, kid-friendly Hole-in-the-Rock trail to a natural opening overlooking the city.
One of the largest city parks in the U.S., with desert hiking trails and a scenic drive to Dobbins Lookout over the Phoenix valley.

a.n: Japanese Friendship Garden of Phoenix (Ro Ho En)
a.d: Three-and-a-half-acre Japanese stroll garden in central Phoenix with a koi pond, waterfall, stone lanterns and a tea house.

a.n: Hall of Flame Museum of Firefighting
a.d: Large firefighting museum with over 130 restored fire engines and equipment from 1725 to modern times, plus a kids' play area.
a.l: 6101 E Van Buren St, Phoenix, AZ 85008

a.n: Wildlife World Zoo, Aquarium & Safari Park
a.d: Day trip · about 35 km from Phoenix. Large West Valley zoo and aquarium with giraffes, rhinos, big cats, a safari train and walk-through aquariums.
a.l: 16501 W Northern Ave, Litchfield Park, AZ 85340

a.d: Day trip · about 85 km from Phoenix. Arizona's oldest and largest botanical garden, with desert plant collections, a lake and trails along Queen Creek below Picketpost Mountain.
Day trip · about 55 km from Phoenix. Maricopa County park on a large desert reservoir north of Phoenix with boating, scenic overlooks, trails and a visitor center.
a.l: 41835 N Castle Hot Springs Rd, Morristown, AZ 85342

a.d: Day trip · about 30 km from Phoenix. Volunteer-run outdoor museum in Chandler with historic locomotives and passenger cars from Arizona's railroads.
The Southwest's largest aquarium: 6,000 animals across 65 exhibits, touch pools, and penguin encounters.
City park with a miniature train ride around the grounds, a 1950s carousel, railroad museum buildings and big playgrounds.
a.l: 7301 E Indian Bend Rd, Scottsdale, AZ 85250

a.d: Scottsdale's huge protected Sonoran Desert preserve with over 200 miles of trails; the Gateway trailhead has easy loops and routes toward Thompson Peak.
a.l: 18333 N Thompson Peak Pkwy, Scottsdale, AZ 85255

a.n: Western Spirit: Scottsdale's Museum of the West
a.d: Smithsonian-affiliated museum in Old Town Scottsdale on the history and art of the American West, from Native American artifacts to cowboy gear.
Day trip · about 40 km from Scottsdale. State park at the foot of the Superstition Mountains with desert hiking trails, wildflowers in spring and views of the rugged peaks.
a.l: 6109 N Apache Trail, Apache Junction, AZ 85119

a.d: Day trip · about 30 km from Scottsdale. Large Maricopa County desert park northeast of Scottsdale with hiking, biking and horse trails and views of the McDowell Mountains and Four Peaks.
a.l: 16300 McDowell Mountain Park Dr, Fountain Hills, AZ 85268

a.d: Day trip · about 35 km from Scottsdale. Reservoir on the Salt River in Tonto National Forest surrounded by saguaro-covered canyon walls, with a marina and boat rentals and tours.
a.l: Saguaro Lake Marina, 14011 N Bush Hwy, Mesa, AZ 85215

a.d: Lakeside park in Fountain Hills whose famous fountain shoots a jet of water hundreds of feet high for 15 minutes every hour during the day.
a.l: 12925 N Saguaro Blvd, Fountain Hills, AZ 85268

a.d: Small free history museum in Scottsdale's 1910 red-brick schoolhouse on the Civic Center mall, telling the town's pioneer story.
Day trip · about 30 km from Scottsdale. Desert park in east Mesa with the Wind Cave trail up Pass Mountain, nature trails and a nature center.
a.l: 3939 N Usery Pass Rd, Mesa, AZ 85207
